blocks.content: Land Degradation Neutrality is a state whereby the amount and quality of land resources necessary to support ecosystem functions and services remain stable or increase within specified temporal and spatial scales.

rows: Restricted strictly to drylands (arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid regions)
Applies universally to all land regions and ecological zones globally
Overgrazing, deforestation, and unsustainable farming in moisture-deficient zones
Soil erosion, chemical contamination, salinization, and urban expansion across all climates
Specifically addressed under the UNCCD framework
Covered under broader SDG targets (SDG 15) and FAO conservation guidelines

items: UNCCD is the only legally binding international agreement linking environment and development to sustainable land management.
Water erosion constitutes the single largest contributor to land degradation in India, a recurring statement in prelims conceptual questions.
Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 15.3 specifically aims to combat desertification and restore degraded land and soil to achieve a land degradation-neutral world by 2030.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Desertification is the degradation of land in arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities.
According to ISRO's Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas, approximately 29.77% of India's Total Geographical Area (TGA) is undergoing land degradation.
Water erosion is the primary driver of land degradation in India, followed by vegetation degradation and wind erosion.
India is a party to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and is committed to achieving Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) by 2030.
Under the Bonn Challenge commitment, India pledged to restore 26 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2030.
